But, as I was trying to explain, you must not imagine I was not affected. Had you been here yesterday evening, just as the lamps were being lit, you would have found me quite distraught. Even Cassian, who was with me, who had in fact conveyed the final message, had no inkling of the turmoil within me. I was utterly wretched. Then it passed. I cannot sustain an emotion; it is a terribly draining exercise. Only the truly sentimental can manage it. And you are being dreadfully unfair, Arthur. You come to my rooms to offer solace. That is so like you. You find me perfectly serene, and you become incensed. What a perfectly sympathetic creature you are! You are like a physician I once heard Cassian describe, a man who devoted his life to finding a cure for some trivial malady. When he at last succeeded, he was inconsolable. His purpose was gone, he was bored beyond all endurance, and took up politics as a final, desperate vice. And besides, my dearest Arthur, if you truly wish to comfort me, you should teach me to see the whole affair as a piece of music, with its inevitable dissonant chord now resolved. Was it not your own favourite poet who wrote of the perfect solace of form? I recall finding a slim, leather-bound volume on your piano once and stumbling upon that very idea. Well, I am not that foolish boy we knew at Cambridge, the one who claimed that a particular harmony in C minor could mend a broken heart. I prefer beauty that one can possess. Fine silks, old malachite, enamelled snuff boxes, Turkish carpets, the decadent gleam of polished rosewood, the sheer luxury of it all, there is a great deal to be said for these things. But the state of mind they engender, or at least permit, is what I value most. To become a critic of one’s own life, as Cassian says, is to be insulated from its crudeness. I can see you are astonished to hear me speak this way. You have not grasped how I have changed. I was a boy when you knew me best. I am a man. I have new appetites, new theories, new philosophies. I am altered, but you must not care for me any less. I have evolved, but you must remain my friend. Of course, I am devoted to Cassian. But I know you are better than he is. You are not wiser, you are too afraid of experience, but you are better. And think how happy we once were! Do not abandon me, Arthur, and do not lecture me. I am what I am. There is nothing else to say.”

The composer felt a strange pang of pity. The young man was still terribly dear to him, and their friendship had been the great inspiration of his recent work. He could not bring himself to chastise him further. After all, this coldness was surely just a pose, a fashionable veneer that would soon wear away. There was so much in him that was good, so much that was fine.

“Very well, Julian,” he said at last, with a tired smile, “I will not speak to you again about this dreadful business, after today. I only hope your name is not dragged through the papers. I hear her family is quite litigious. Have they contacted you?”

Julian shook his head, and a shadow of irritation crossed his features at the mention of lawyers. There was something so common and grubby about legal matters. “They do not know my surname,” he answered.

“But surely Eleanor did?”

“Only my Christian name, and I am certain she never told a soul. She confessed to me once that her sisters were desperate to know who I was, and she always told them my name was Apollo. It was a charming little fancy of hers. You must compose a sonata for me about Eleanor, Arthur. I should like to have something more of her than the memory of a few hurried meetings and a great many tearful letters.”

“I will see what I can do, Julian, if it would give you pleasure. But you must come to the studio again. The automaton is not quite finished without you.”

“I can never come to your studio again, Arthur. It is impossible!” he cried, springing up from the chaise-longue.

The composer stared at him. “My dear boy, what absurdity!” he said. “Do you mean you are displeased with my work? Where is it? Why have you thrown that dreadful cashmere shawl over its cage? Let me see it. It is the finest thing I have ever made. Do take the shawl away, Julian. It is a crime for your man to hide my creation like that. I knew the room felt different when I entered.”

“My valet has nothing to do with it, Arthur. You cannot think I allow him to meddle with my treasures? He arranges my cravats for me on occasion, that is all. No; I did it myself. The morning sun was too bright upon the silverwork.”

“Too bright! Hardly, my dear fellow. It is the perfect spot for it. Let me look.” And Arthur strode towards the alcove by the window.

A cry of pure panic broke from Julian’s lips, and he rushed to place himself between the composer and the draped cage. “Arthur,” he said, his face quite pale, “you must not look at it. I forbid you to.”

“Not look at my own automaton! You cannot be serious. Why should I not look at it?” exclaimed Arthur, with a short laugh.

“If you try to look at it, Arthur, on my word of honour I will never receive you in my home again. I am entirely serious. I offer no reason, and you are not to demand one. But, be warned, if you so much as touch that shawl, our friendship is at an end.”

Arthur was dumbfounded. He looked at Julian in utter bewilderment. He had never seen him in such a state. The young man was positively white with fury. His hands were balled into fists, and his eyes, usually so placid, were like chips of sapphire ice. He was trembling from head to foot.

“Julian!”

“Do not speak!”

“But what is the meaning of this? Of course I will not look at it if you do not wish me to,” he said, somewhat stiffly, turning on his heel and walking back towards the fireplace. “But, truly, it seems rather ridiculous that I should not be allowed to inspect my own work, particularly as it is to be presented at the Crystal Palace next month. I shall likely need to make some adjustments to the mechanism before then, so I must see it someday, and why not today?”

“To present it! You mean to present it?” exclaimed Julian, a strange new terror seizing him. Was the world to be shown his secret? Were crowds of common people to peer at the mystery of his life? That was unthinkable. Something, he knew not what, must be done immediately.

“Yes; I cannot imagine you would object. The Prince’s committee is gathering the greatest marvels of engineering for a grand exhibition in May. The automaton will only be gone for a fortnight. I should think you could bear to part with it for that long. Indeed, if you keep it perpetually hidden, you cannot care for it very much.”

Julian ran a hand across his brow. There were beads of sweat there. He felt that he was on the precipice of some ghastly danger. “You told me weeks ago that you would never show it to anyone,” he cried. “Why have you altered your decision? You people who pride yourselves on consistency are as fickle as anyone else. The only difference is that your whims are so terribly earnest. You cannot have forgotten that you promised me, most solemnly, that nothing on earth would persuade you to make it a public spectacle. You told Cassian the very same thing.” He stopped, and a sudden spark ignited in his eyes. He recalled something Cassian had said to him once, half in jest and half in earnest, “If you desire a truly singular afternoon, persuade Arthur to tell you why he will not explain his inventions. He told me why he refused to patent the automaton, and it was a revelation.” Yes, perhaps Arthur, too, had his secret. He would press him, and see.

“Arthur,” he said, moving very close and looking him directly in the face, “we each have a secret, it seems. Let me know yours, and I shall tell you mine. What was your reason for refusing to patent the automaton?”

The composer flinched, almost imperceptibly. “Julian, if I told you, you might think less of me than you do now.”

This secret that he had built up in his mind into something strange and dark was, at its heart, merely a piece of artistic vanity. A fear of being misunderstood, a high-minded terror of the vulgar crowd. It seemed so trivial, so terribly insignificant compared to the monstrous miracle that was taking place behind the Indian shawl. The automaton was not a diary of Arthur’s intellect; it was becoming the diary of Julian’s soul, and it was writing its entries in lines of sin and degradation.

Then, this wave of bitterness passed, and a flicker of cunning, subtle and sharp, took its place. He saw his advantage. He saw the path open before him, clear and certain. He walked towards Arthur, his expression one of profound sympathy.

“I see now,” he said, his voice soft and musical. “I see it all. Then the automaton is not really mine at all, is it, Arthur? If it contains so much of you, it is yours. I am merely its guardian. How could I have been so selfish? You have put your very soul into it, as you say. A masterpiece into which you have woven your dreams. I have often heard Cassian say that the true artist is the one who is least himself in his art, for his art has taken all that is essential. The automaton has taken your essence. Therefore, it belongs to you, not to me.”

“Julian, what are you saying?” Arthur murmured, confused by this sudden turn. “Of course it is yours. I made it for you. It was a gift.”

“A gift of yourself,” Julian insisted, pressing his point. “And a man has the right to do as he pleases with his own soul. So let us make a bargain. You wish to see it. I can understand that. An artist must look upon his work. But you must understand my position, as well. Cassian has filled my head with his strange philosophies, with the idea that certain things are too beautiful to be shared, that their perfection is kept intact only by secrecy. Let me have my whim. You must choose. Either you look at it now, tear away this shawl and satisfy your curiosity and your pride as its creator, and we shall be as strangers from this moment forth. Our friendship will be a thing of the past, a memory like any other. Or… you trust me. You trust in my friendship, which you have always praised, and you give me your word that you will never again ask to look upon the automaton. You will let it remain my secret. In return, I will be your friend for ever. The most loyal friend you have ever had.”

Arthur stared at him, aghast. “A choice like that! It is no choice at all! It is monstrous, Julian!”

His artist’s pride warred with his affection. It was his greatest creation; it was his right to see it, to tend to it, to ensure it was perfect. To be denied a look at his own work was an insult beyond measure. And yet, the thought of losing Julian was a desolation. The boy’s companionship had become a necessary luxury, a brilliant light in the often grey and methodical world of his own mind. To be cast out, to have that door closed to him forever, seemed a price too terrible to pay for the satisfaction of a moment. He saw the cold finality in Julian’s eyes and knew that he was not being dramatic; he was in deadly earnest.

“You are serious,” Arthur said, his voice hoarse. “You would truly end our friendship over this.”

“Everything is over between us if you do not give me your word,” Julian repeated, his tone unwavering.

Arthur passed a hand over his eyes, as if to ward off a sudden pain. He felt old and weary. The boy’s strange mood, this inexplicable stubbornness, was a mystery he could not solve. Perhaps it was, as Julian had said, merely a passing whim, a new philosophy he had adopted and would discard in a month. To fight it would be to shatter something he held infinitely dear.

“So be it,” he said at last, with a deep, shuddering sigh. He let his hand fall and tried to smile, but it was a sad, twisted thing. “Let the automaton have its secret. “You will come to the studio soon?” he asked. “The light is perfect in the mornings.”

“Of course, my dear Arthur. Whenever you wish.”

“And you are not… you are not angry with me?”

“Angry with you!” Julian exclaimed. “My dearest friend, my one true friend, how could I be angry with you? I am only grateful. You have trusted me, and I shall not forget it.”

“You rang, sir?”

“Yes, Fletcher. I need your assistance. And that of one of the footmen. I wish for something to be moved.”

“Very good, sir. To where?”

“Do you remember the old playroom, at the very top of the house?”

Fletcher looked thoughtful. “The one with the barred window, sir? I believe it has been locked for a great many years. Since you were a boy.”

“Precisely. I wish to use it for storage. Find the key. I believe my solicitor, Mr. Harmsworth, has a list of them. Send a message to him at once. I require that key this evening. Then you and I and one other man will carry something up there for me.”

“Carry what, sir?” asked the valet, his gaze travelling, as if by instinct, to the shrouded object in the corner.

“This,” Julian said, gesturing towards it. “This automaton. It is… a little in the way down here. I should like it to be put somewhere safe. Somewhere it will not be disturbed.”

“Very good, sir. I shall see to the key immediately.”

When the valet had gone, Julian was alone with his secret once more. He felt a fierce surge of possessiveness. He had defended it. He had saved it from the world, from the prying eyes of its own creator. It was his, and his alone.

He lit a cigarette, the flare of the match illuminating his face for a second, showing it pale but resolute. He could not leave it here another night. The risk was too great. Arthur might change his mind. Cassian might call, in one of his inquisitive moods. No, it had to be hidden away, locked in that forgotten room of his childhood, a place of ghosts and memories. There was a grim poetry in it that appealed to him. The sins of his manhood were to be locked away in the chamber of his innocence.

He walked to the corner and, with a hand that did not tremble in the slightest, he once again pulled away the heavy Indian shawl.

The automaton sat there in its inscrutable perfection. The afternoon light, now turning a deep gold, burnished the bronze of its limbs and glinted on the silver filigree of its waistcoat. For a moment, it seemed unchanged, as perfect and as impassive as the day Arthur had delivered it. Julian leaned closer, his eyes searching the placid, metallic face for the secret it held.

And then he saw it.

It was not a great change. A stranger would not have noticed it. Even Arthur, perhaps, in a casual glance, might have missed it. But Julian saw. There was a faint, metallic gleam of cunning in the crystal eyes, a subtle shift in their lustre that had not been there an hour before. They seemed to watch him with a kind of cold, calculating intelligence. And there was something else. He looked at the hands, those marvels of articulation that could hold a pen or a flower with such delicate precision. The articulated fingers of its right hand, which had before been resting in a state of perfect, relaxed grace upon its knee, were now tensed, almost imperceptibly. The metal digits were curved in a subtle, predatory arc, as if the thing were on the verge of grasping something, or of crushing it.

A shiver of mingled horror and delight passed through Julian. So, it was true. It was not his imagination. The thing was living his life for him, and it was taking on the reflection of his own soul. The lie he had told Arthur, the cruel choice he had presented, the triumphant scorn he had felt—they were all there, written in the faintest of traces upon the unbreathing thing before him.

He felt as though he had been watching a play, and a thrill of artistic pleasure was shot through with a chilling premonition of the drama yet to come. The automaton would bear the burden of his passions, the scars of his experience. He could remain young, and beautiful, and untouched.

He heard the sound of footsteps ascending the stairs. It was Fletcher, returning with the footman. With a final, lingering look at the faint, new line of tension in the automaton’s hand, Julian threw the shawl over it, shrouding it once more in shadow and silk. He was ready. The secret was safe.
